title: Complete Grant Writing & Fundraising Professional Certificate
description: A full 20-module program from beginner to professional grant writer & fundraising specialist: finding funding, organizational readiness, needs assessment, proposal writing, project planning, budgeting, review & submission, fundraising, digital fundraising, donor relations, grant management, M&E, technology & AI, career, 10 real-world proposals, a capstone and a Certificate of Completion.
outcomes: Identify funding opportunities and read grant guidelines
Conduct needs assessments and write winning grant proposals
Develop logframes, work plans, budgets and budget justifications
Design fundraising strategies and run digital fundraising campaigns
Build donor relationships and manage grant-funded projects
Monitor, evaluate and report to donors — and build a portfolio & career
about: This is the complete TIH Grant Writing & Fundraising Professional Certificate, rebuilt into twenty modules that take you from the basics to professional practice.

Every content lesson has a video and formal detailed study notes; downloadable templates cover the Grant Proposal, Budget, Logframe, Concept Note, Needs Assessment, Gantt chart, Donor Report, Fundraising Plan and M&E Framework, and ten real-world proposals plus a capstone build your portfolio.

Software & tools: Microsoft Word/Excel/PowerPoint, Google Docs/Sheets/Forms, Canva, ChatGPT, Trello, Asana, Notion and Salesforce for Nonprofits. You finish with a portfolio and — after the graduation assessment — a Certificate of Completion.
requirements: No prior experience required — we start from the basics
A device with a word processor and spreadsheet
Willingness to write real or sample proposals and budgets

faqs.question: Is this course really free, and do I get a certificate?
faqs.answer: Yes, completely free, no credit card required. When you pass the final assessment you receive a verifiable TIH certificate (ID format TIH-2026-GRW-XXXX) that you can show to employers, NGOs, and donor-funded projects hiring grants staff.

faqs.question: Do I need to work for a registered NGO to benefit?
faqs.answer: No. The course serves NGO staff, community group leaders, students, and freelancers. Grant writing is also a paid skill, many Liberian organizations hire consultants to write proposals, and this course prepares you for that work.

faqs.question: Will this help me win grants specifically in Liberia?
faqs.answer: Yes. Every module uses West African examples: donors active in Liberia (USAID, EU, UNDP, UNICEF, Mastercard Foundation), budgets in USD and LRD, mobile money considerations, and the realities of community projects in Monrovia and the counties.

faqs.question: How long does the course take and what is the capstone?
faqs.answer: About 20 hours total, most learners finish in 3-4 weeks studying an hour a day. The capstone asks you to write a complete, realistic $10,000 grant proposal (needs statement, logic model, objectives, budget, and M&E plan) that you can adapt and submit to a real donor.

instructor.name: Miatta S. Freeman
instructor.title: Grants & Partnerships Director, West Africa Impact Alliance
instructor.bio: Miatta S. Freeman has raised over $4.2 million for Liberian and West African NGOs, winning grants from USAID, the EU, UNDP, and the Mastercard Foundation. Based in Monrovia, she has trained hundreds of community organizations from Paynesville to Ganta in professional proposal development.

lessons.title: 1.1 Welcome to the Course
lessons.html:
Grant Writing & FundraisingModule 1: Course Orientation
LESSON NOTE: WELCOME TO THE COURSE
SubjectGrant Writing & Fundraising
TopicWelcome to the Course
LevelBeginner to Professional
Lesson duration45–60 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • Explain Welcome to the Course in clear, simple language.
  • Describe why it matters in grant writing and fundraising foundations.
  • Apply the correct process to a realistic organisation or community project.
  • Recognise weak practice and improve it to a professional standard.

1. Introduction

Winning support is not about using impressive words. It is about helping a funder understand a real need, trust the proposed solution, and see that the applicant can deliver and account for the money. This lesson explains Welcome to the Course as a practical skill you can use.

2. Meaning and definition

Definition: The Complete Grant Writing & Fundraising Professional Certificate is a structured programme that trains learners to identify funding opportunities, write competitive proposals, manage grants, and design effective fundraising strategies.

In simple terms, this topic answers an important professional question: what must the writer or fundraiser know, decide, show, or do at this stage?

3. How to apply it

  1. Understand the purpose. Identify the decision the funder, donor, manager, or community must make.
  2. Gather reliable information. Use guidelines, organisational records, credible data, quotations, or consultation instead of guesses.
  3. Prepare the work. Understand the purpose, follow a clear process, apply it to a realistic organisation, and check the work against professional standards.
  4. Check alignment. Make sure the information agrees with the proposal’s need, objectives, activities, results, timeline and budget.
  5. Review for clarity and ethics. Remove exaggeration, explain assumptions and verify names, dates, figures and claims.

4. Worked example

Example: A community organisation in Monrovia reads the funder’s instructions, confirms that its education project is eligible, uses local evidence, writes measurable results, and checks that the work plan and budget agree before submission.

5. Weak practice and professional practice

Weak approachProfessional approach
Uses vague claims, copies general language, ignores the funder’s instructions, or leaves important decisions unexplained.Uses specific evidence, plain language, realistic figures, clear responsibility, and content tailored to the funder and community.

6. Practical task

Apply it: Prepare a short example of Welcome to the Course for a real or realistic Liberian NGO, school, community group, social enterprise, health project, agriculture project, or youth programme.

7. How to answer a professional or assessment question

Begin with a direct definition. Explain the purpose and the steps in a logical order. Add one realistic example and show how the work connects to donor requirements. If the question says compare, give both similarities and differences; if it says evaluate, give strengths, weaknesses and a justified conclusion.

8. Summary

  • Welcome to the Course is part of grant writing and fundraising foundations.
  • Good work is specific, evidence-based, ethical and aligned.
  • Every claim, activity and cost should be understandable and verifiable.
  • Professional writers revise their work against the funder’s exact instructions.

9. Key terms

TermMeaning
Welcome to the CourseThe Complete Grant Writing & Fundraising Professional Certificate is a structured programme that trains learners to identify funding opportunities, write competitive proposals, manage grants, and design effective fundraising strategies.
AlignmentThe match between the project, the applicant and the funder’s priorities.
EvidenceReliable information used to support a statement or decision.
ComplianceFollowing the funder’s rules, conditions and required format.

10. Review questions

1. Which approach is most professional?

Answer: Use evidence, follow the guidelines, explain decisions and tailor the work to the funder. Why: Donors need clear, credible and relevant information.

2. Why should this topic connect to the rest of the proposal?

Answer: Because the need, objectives, activities, results, timeline and budget must describe the same project. Contradictions reduce confidence.

  1. Define Welcome to the Course in your own words.
  2. Give one example of weak practice and explain how you would improve it.
  3. How could a Liberian community organisation apply this lesson?

11. Class activities

  1. Improve the weak version: Write a vague two-sentence example, exchange it with a classmate, and improve it by adding evidence, clarity and alignment.
  2. Funder review: Choose a real or sample funding guideline and identify where this topic appears in the requirements or scoring criteria.

12. Assignment

Prepare a one-page application of Welcome to the Course for a realistic project. Include the organisation, target group, location, evidence used, your main decisions, and a short checklist showing how your work meets professional standards.

Grant Writing & FundraisingModule 6: Proposal Writing Fundamentals
LESSON NOTE: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
SubjectGrant Writing & Fundraising
TopicExecutive Summary
LevelBeginner to Professional
Lesson duration45–60 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • Explain Executive Summary in clear, simple language.
  • Describe why it matters in professional proposal writing.
  • Apply the correct process to a realistic organisation or community project.
  • Recognise weak practice and improve it to a professional standard.

1. Introduction

Winning support is not about using impressive words. It is about helping a funder understand a real need, trust the proposed solution, and see that the applicant can deliver and account for the money. This lesson explains Executive Summary as a practical skill you can use.

2. Meaning and definition

Definition: An executive summary is a concise overview, usually one page or less, that presents the essential elements of a proposal so that a reviewer can quickly grasp the request and its importance.

In simple terms, this topic answers an important professional question: what must the writer or fundraiser know, decide, show, or do at this stage?

3. How to apply it

  1. Understand the purpose. Identify the decision the funder, donor, manager, or community must make.
  2. Gather reliable information. Use guidelines, organisational records, credible data, quotations, or consultation instead of guesses.
  3. Prepare the work. Connect the need, objectives, activities, timeline, results and budget so that each section tells one consistent story.
  4. Check alignment. Make sure the information agrees with the proposal’s need, objectives, activities, results, timeline and budget.
  5. Review for clarity and ethics. Remove exaggeration, explain assumptions and verify names, dates, figures and claims.

4. Worked example

Example: A community organisation in Monrovia reads the funder’s instructions, confirms that its education project is eligible, uses local evidence, writes measurable results, and checks that the work plan and budget agree before submission.

5. Weak practice and professional practice

Weak approachProfessional approach
Uses vague claims, copies general language, ignores the funder’s instructions, or leaves important decisions unexplained.Uses specific evidence, plain language, realistic figures, clear responsibility, and content tailored to the funder and community.

6. Practical template

📥 Template: Concept Note

  • Title & organization
  • Problem / need (brief)
  • Proposed solution & objectives
  • Target beneficiaries
  • Approximate budget & duration
  • Expected impact

Offline use: Choose Print → Save as PDF to keep a copy.

7. How to answer a professional or assessment question

Begin with a direct definition. Explain the purpose and the steps in a logical order. Add one realistic example and show how the work connects to donor requirements. If the question says compare, give both similarities and differences; if it says evaluate, give strengths, weaknesses and a justified conclusion.

8. Summary

  • Executive Summary is part of professional proposal writing.
  • Good work is specific, evidence-based, ethical and aligned.
  • Every claim, activity and cost should be understandable and verifiable.
  • Professional writers revise their work against the funder’s exact instructions.

TermMeaning
Executive SummaryAn executive summary is a concise overview, usually one page or less, that presents the essential elements of a proposal so that a reviewer can quickly grasp the request and its importance.
AlignmentThe match between the project, the applicant and the funder’s priorities.
EvidenceReliable information used to support a statement or decision.
ComplianceFollowing the funder’s rules, conditions and required format.

10. Review questions

1. Which approach is most professional?

Answer: Use evidence, follow the guidelines, explain decisions and tailor the work to the funder. Why: Donors need clear, credible and relevant information.

2. Why should this topic connect to the rest of the proposal?

Answer: Because the need, objectives, activities, results, timeline and budget must describe the same project. Contradictions reduce confidence.

  1. Define Executive Summary in your own words.
  2. Give one example of weak practice and explain how you would improve it.
  3. How could a Liberian community organisation apply this lesson?

  1. Improve the weak version: Write a vague two-sentence example, exchange it with a classmate, and improve it by adding evidence, clarity and alignment.
  2. Funder review: Choose a real or sample funding guideline and identify where this topic appears in the requirements or scoring criteria.

Prepare a one-page application of Executive Summary for a realistic project. Include the organisation, target group, location, evidence used, your main decisions, and a short checklist showing how your work meets professional standards.

  • Apply the correct process to a realistic organisation or community project.

1. Introduction

Winning support is not about using impressive words. It is about helping a funder understand a real need, trust the proposed solution, and see that the applicant can deliver and account for the money. This lesson explains Budget Review as a practical skill you can use.

2. Meaning and definition

Definition: Budget Review is a practical skill used to plan, finance, communicate, or manage mission-driven work.

In simple terms, this topic answers an important professional question: what must the writer or fundraiser know, decide, show, or do at this stage?

3. How to apply it

  1. Understand the purpose. Identify the decision the funder, donor, manager, or community must make.
  2. Gather reliable information. Use guidelines, organisational records, credible data, quotations, or consultation instead of guesses.
  3. Prepare the work. List each necessary cost, calculate it from clear units and rates, and confirm that every cost supports an activity.
  4. Check alignment. Make sure the information agrees with the proposal’s need, objectives, activities, results, timeline and budget.
  5. Review for clarity and ethics. Remove exaggeration, explain assumptions and verify names, dates, figures and claims.

4. Worked example

Example: A youth skills project plans to train 50 learners. Instead of writing “training: US$2,000,” the writer shows 2 trainers × 5 days × US$100 = US$1,000, materials at US$10 × 50 learners = US$500, and venue at US$100 × 5 days = US$500.

5. Weak practice and professional practice

Weak approachProfessional approach
Uses vague claims, copies general language, ignores the funder’s instructions, or leaves important decisions unexplained.Uses specific evidence, plain language, realistic figures, clear responsibility, and content tailored to the funder and community.

📥 Template: Budget

  • Personnel (roles, % time, cost)
  • Equipment & supplies
  • Operational/programme costs
  • Indirect/overhead costs

  • Totals per year and grand total

EvidenceReliable information used to support a statement or decision.
ComplianceFollowing the funder’s rules, conditions and required format.

1. Which approach is most professional?

Learning objectives

  • Describe why it matters in proposal review and submission.
  • Apply the correct process to a realistic organisation or community project.
  • Recognise weak practice and improve it to a professional standard.

1. Introduction

Winning support is not about using impressive words. It is about helping a funder understand a real need, trust the proposed solution, and see that the applicant can deliver and account for the money. This lesson explains Submission Portals as a practical skill you can use.

2. Meaning and definition

Definition: Submission Portals is a practical skill used to plan, finance, communicate, or manage mission-driven work.

In simple terms, this topic answers an important professional question: what must the writer or fundraiser know, decide, show, or do at this stage?

3. How to apply it

  1. Understand the purpose. Identify the decision the funder, donor, manager, or community must make.
  2. Gather reliable information. Use guidelines, organisational records, credible data, quotations, or consultation instead of guesses.
  3. Prepare the work. Check alignment and eligibility first, record every requirement and deadline, then decide whether the opportunity is worth pursuing.
  4. Check alignment. Make sure the information agrees with the proposal’s need, objectives, activities, results, timeline and budget.
  5. Review for clarity and ethics. Remove exaggeration, explain assumptions and verify names, dates, figures and claims.

4. Worked example

Example: A community organisation in Monrovia reads the funder’s instructions, confirms that its education project is eligible, uses local evidence, writes measurable results, and checks that the work plan and budget agree before submission.

5. Weak practice and professional practice

Weak approachProfessional approach
Uses vague claims, copies general language, ignores the funder’s instructions, or leaves important decisions unexplained.Uses specific evidence, plain language, realistic figures, clear responsibility, and content tailored to the funder and community.

6. Practical task

Apply it: Prepare a short example of Submission Portals for a real or realistic Liberian NGO, school, community group, social enterprise, health project, agriculture project, or youth programme.

7. How to answer a professional or assessment question

Begin with a direct definition. Explain the purpose and the steps in a logical order. Add one realistic example and show how the work connects to donor requirements. If the question says compare, give both similarities and differences; if it says evaluate, give strengths, weaknesses and a justified conclusion.

8. Summary

  • Submission Portals is part of proposal review and submission.
  • Good work is specific, evidence-based, ethical and aligned.
  • Every claim, activity and cost should be understandable and verifiable.
  • Professional writers revise their work against the funder’s exact instructions.

9. Key terms

TermMeaning
Submission PortalsSubmission Portals is a practical skill used to plan, finance, communicate, or manage mission-driven work.
AlignmentThe match between the project, the applicant and the funder’s priorities.
EvidenceReliable information used to support a statement or decision.
ComplianceFollowing the funder’s rules, conditions and required format.

1. Which approach is most professional?

Answer: Use evidence, follow the guidelines, explain decisions and tailor the work to the funder. Why: Donors need clear, credible and relevant information.

2. Why should this topic connect to the rest of the proposal?

Answer: Because the need, objectives, activities, results, timeline and budget must describe the same project. Contradictions reduce confidence.

  1. Define Submission Portals in your own words.
  2. Give one example of weak practice and explain how you would improve it.
  3. How could a Liberian community organisation apply this lesson?

LESSON NOTE: SMS FUNDRAISING
SubjectGrant Writing & Fundraising
TopicSMS Fundraising
LevelBeginner to Professional
Lesson duration45–60 minutes

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • Explain SMS Fundraising in clear, simple language.
  • Describe why it matters in digital fundraising.
  • Apply the correct process to a realistic organisation or community project.
  • Recognise weak practice and improve it to a professional standard.

1. Introduction

Winning support is not about using impressive words. It is about helping a funder understand a real need, trust the proposed solution, and see that the applicant can deliver and account for the money. This lesson explains SMS Fundraising as a practical skill you can use.

2. Meaning and definition

Definition: SMS Fundraising is a practical skill used to plan, finance, communicate, or manage mission-driven work.

In simple terms, this topic answers an important professional question: what must the writer or fundraiser know, decide, show, or do at this stage?

3. How to apply it

  1. Understand the purpose. Identify the decision the funder, donor, manager, or community must make.
  2. Gather reliable information. Use guidelines, organisational records, credible data, quotations, or consultation instead of guesses.
  3. Prepare the work. Identify the audience, understand what they care about, make a clear and respectful request, and plan how the relationship will be maintained.
  4. Check alignment. Make sure the information agrees with the proposal’s need, objectives, activities, results, timeline and budget.
  5. Review for clarity and ethics. Remove exaggeration, explain assumptions and verify names, dates, figures and claims.

4. Worked example

Example: A Liberian education organisation researches a company’s community priorities before requesting support, presents a specific student-learning result, thanks the donor promptly, and later reports what the contribution achieved.

5. Weak practice and professional practice

Weak approachProfessional approach
Uses vague claims, copies general language, ignores the funder’s instructions, or leaves important decisions unexplained.Uses specific evidence, plain language, realistic figures, clear responsibility, and content tailored to the funder and community.

6. Practical task

Apply it: Prepare a short example of SMS Fundraising for a real or realistic Liberian NGO, school, community group, social enterprise, health project, agriculture project, or youth programme.

7. How to answer a professional or assessment question

Begin with a direct definition. Explain the purpose and the steps in a logical order. Add one realistic example and show how the work connects to donor requirements. If the question says compare, give both similarities and differences; if it says evaluate, give strengths, weaknesses and a justified conclusion.

8. Summary

  • SMS Fundraising is part of digital fundraising.
  • Good work is specific, evidence-based, ethical and aligned.
  • Every claim, activity and cost should be understandable and verifiable.
  • Professional writers revise their work against the funder’s exact instructions.

9. Key terms

TermMeaning
SMS FundraisingSMS Fundraising is a practical skill used to plan, finance, communicate, or manage mission-driven work.
AlignmentThe match between the project, the applicant and the funder’s priorities.
EvidenceReliable information used to support a statement or decision.
ComplianceFollowing the funder’s rules, conditions and required format.

10. Review questions

1. Which approach is most professional?

Answer: Use evidence, follow the guidelines, explain decisions and tailor the work to the funder. Why: Donors need clear, credible and relevant information.

2. Why should this topic connect to the rest of the proposal?

Answer: Because the need, objectives, activities, results, timeline and budget must describe the same project. Contradictions reduce confidence.

  1. Define SMS Fundraising in your own words.
  2. Give one example of weak practice and explain how you would improve it.
  3. How could a Liberian community organisation apply this lesson?

11. Class activities

  1. Improve the weak version: Write a vague two-sentence example, exchange it with a classmate, and improve it by adding evidence, clarity and alignment.
  2. Funder review: Choose a real or sample funding guideline and identify where this topic appears in the requirements or scoring criteria.

Prepare a one-page application of SMS Fundraising for a realistic project. Include the organisation, target group, location, evidence used, your main decisions, and a short checklist showing how your work meets professional standards.

questions.question: The executive summary should:

questions.explanation: The grant agreement sets the formal terms.

questions.question: A grant is:
options: Funds given (usually not repaid) for a specific purpose
questions.explanation: Grants fund a purpose and generally are not repaid.

questions.question: Goals differ from objectives in that goals are:
options: Broad; objectives are specific and measurable
questions.explanation: Goals are broad; objectives are specific steps.

questions.question: International development grants often focus on:
options: Poverty reduction, health, education and sustainable development
questions.explanation: They target development outcomes.

questions.question: The grant life cycle includes:
questions.explanation: It spans finding, applying, implementing and reporting.

questions.question: Corporate grants are typically linked to:
options: Corporate social responsibility or strategic community interests
questions.explanation: They often support CSR or business-aligned causes.

questions.question: Grant writing is the process of:
options: Preparing proposals to secure funding from donors
questions.explanation: Grant writing seeks funding through written proposals.

lessons.title: 20.1 Certificate Requirements
lessons.html:
Module 20: Assessments & GraduationGraduation

Certificate Requirements

To graduate and earn your TIH Certificate of Completion you must:

  • Complete the lessons in Modules 1–17.
  • Complete the real-world proposals in Module 18 (10 projects).
  • Complete the capstone grant proposal in Module 19 and present it.
  • Pass the skill assessments, the Midterm and Final Examinations, the Capstone Evaluation and the Portfolio Review.
  • Pass the final Certificate of Completion assessment.
